section_summary: This section covers U.S. diplomatic and intelligence reporting from January to June 1939 regarding Japan's wartime political and economic mobilization under the Hiranuma Cabinet. Key topics include the invocation and extension of the National General Mobilization Law (compulsory vocational registration, corporate dividend controls, and commodity price fixing), bureaucratic and military maneuvering over the Cabinet Planning Board, and the establishment and staffing of the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-In) to administer occupied China. It also contains extensive debates within the Diet over foreign relations, third-power treaty rights, and the 'New Order in East Asia', alongside internal State Department analyses of evolving Japanese state socialism and a consular report on wartime economic boom, civilian morale, and anti-Jewish propaganda in the Kansai region.

subfiles.about: Reports on the implementation of the National General Mobilization Law in Japan, including vocational registration, dividend restrictions, and the reorganization of the Cabinet Planning Board.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the expanding application of the National General Mobilization Law, particularly Article 21 requiring compulsory vocational registration of skilled laborers, technicians, and graduates. The despatch examines political tensions surrounding the reorganization of the Cabinet Planning Board and disputes between the Ministry of Finance and the Army over dividend limitations under Article 11. Attached to the despatch are lists of imperial ordinances submitted and unsubmitted to the Mobilization Deliberative Commission, as well as a full English translation of Imperial Ordinance No. 5 concerning vocational registration.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3640: Implementation of Provisions of the National General Mobilization Law

subfiles.about: Transmits an intelligence report regarding the organization and political nature of the Hiranuma Cabinet based on Japanese press sources.
subfiles.summary: Naval Attaché report sheet relays press-based intelligence on the Hiranuma Cabinet's formation and political makeup, forwarded to Naval Operations and State's Far Eastern Division.
subfiles.title: Attaché's Report: The Hiranuma Cabinet

subfiles.about: Summarizes and analyzes Tokyo Despatch No. 3683 concerning Diet criticisms of the Asia Promotion Board's divided control over China policy.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury reviews Despatch 3683: Peers interpellations questioned divided Foreign Office/Asia Promotion Board authority; Hiranuma's defense that the Foreign Minister also serves as Board Vice President seemed unsatisfactory, noting planned regional Board offices.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3683 Regarding the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-In)

subfiles.about: Reports on debates in the House of Peers regarding the administrative friction and jurisdictional division between the Asia Promotion Board and the Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays Yamakawa's Peers criticism of divided China-policy supervision between the Foreign Office and Asia Promotion Board; Hiranuma said diplomacy stays with Foreign Office while economic/cultural coordination goes to the Board, jurisdiction unresolved, with regional branches planned.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3683: Asia Promotion Board (Koa-In)

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 3685 regarding Diet interpellations on foreign relations, the Far Eastern economic bloc, and third-power rights.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury outlines Arita's Lower House replies to Ogawa: combating anti-Japanese sentiment, expecting a new Chinese regime, avoiding 'economic bloc' language while insisting on regional coordination, and addressing British/American Open-Door protests amid a chauvinistic, unconciliatory House mood.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3685 Regarding Diet Debates on Foreign Relations

subfiles.about: Transmits a report and translated Diet proceedings of Foreign Minister Arita's responses to questions on China policy and foreign relations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides an account of the Lower House Diet debate of January 21, 1939, enclosing a complete translation of Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita's reply to interpellations by Gotaro Ogawa. Arita defended Japan's creation of a new order in East Asia, discussed the repercussions of Wang Jingwei's peace move, and acknowledged that closer tripartite economic association would create an inevitable gap with the traditional Open Door policy. Grew notes the strong chauvinism in the Diet and briefly assesses Japanese attitudes toward possible American and British economic sanctions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3685: Debates in the Diet on Japan's Foreign Relations as Affected by Japan's China Policy

subfiles.about: Endorses Salisbury's assessment that Japanese business exerts influence through government bureaucracy rather than opposing the military directly.
subfiles.summary: Sturgeon agrees with Salisbury that an independent Japanese business class can't directly confront the military, since commercial interests exert influence indirectly through government and bureaucracy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Political Influence of Japanese Business and the Military

subfiles.about: Analyzes the shifting power dynamic between the military, civilian bureaucracy, and big business interests in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury rejects claims Japan's bureaucracy is wholly subservient to the military, arguing it may dominate once China gains consolidate, noting Mitsui/Mitsubishi work through party/bureaucratic channels and currently back the military mainly for war profits.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Bureaucracy, Military Dominance, and Capitalist Interests

subfiles.about: Critiques the thesis of Tokyo Despatch No. 3778, arguing that state economic control strengthens rather than weakens military supremacy.
subfiles.summary: Luthringer doubts Grew's view that bureaucracy will erode military dominance, arguing state economic control mainly maximizes military power/autarky, and questioning whether bureaucracy counters the military better than an independent capitalist class.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Social Control of Economic Life and Military Dominance in Japan

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 3778 on the evolution of state socialism, price fixing, and dividend limits under the National Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine reviews Schuler's despatch on expanding state socialism via price/dividend controls and spiritual mobilization, seeing traditional oligarchical checks rather than European fascism, praising its analysis of coming bureaucratic resurgence after continental gains.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3778 Regarding National Mobilization and State Socialism

subfiles.about: Analyzes the expansion of economic controls under the National General Mobilization Law and the unique nature of Japanese state socialism.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the accelerated invocation of the National General Mobilization Law, notably Article 11 restricting corporate dividends to ten percent and Article 19 establishing comprehensive commodity price fixing. He examines the establishment of the National Spiritual Mobilization Committee under the Minister of Education and the political shelving of single-party movement bills by Premier Hiranuma. Grew argues that Japanese state socialism is shaped by historical traditions of oligarchical checks and balances rather than European fascism, suggesting that civilian bureaucracy may ultimately supersede military dominance after the China conflict.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3778: National Mobilization and the Evolution of Socialism in Japan

subfiles.about: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 3786 on the creation and military staffing of China liaison branch offices of the Asia Promotion Board.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine outlines new Asia Promotion Board liaison offices in five cities, dominated by army/navy officers excluding Foreign Office staff, split along North-China-army/South-China-navy lines, previewing a Tokyo conference on puppet regimes and river navigation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3786 Regarding Branch Offices of the Asia Promotion Board

subfiles.about: Reports on the formal authorization, regional jurisdictions, and personnel appointments for branch liaison offices of the Asia Promotion Board in China.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the gazetting of Asia Promotion Board liaison offices in Peiping, Kalgan, Shanghai, Amoy, and Tsingtao, matching existing puppet administrative regimes. He details the appointment of prominent military figures such as Generals Kita, Nemoto, and Sakai, and Admirals Tsuda and Mito to head these offices, observing that the Foreign Office has been largely sidelined. Grew highlights administrative risks of branch chiefs holding ranks equal to Tokyo leaders and previews an April conference in Tokyo on puppet governments, currency problems, and development companies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3786: Establishment of Branch Offices of the Asia Promotion Board (Koa-In)

subfiles.about: Summarizes Consul General Makinson's report on economic conditions, war boom profits, labor shortages, and emerging financial strain in the Kansai region.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury reviews an Osaka report: high morale from war profits and full employment, growing educated-class unease over American-British alignment, and signs Japan was starting to feel economic/financial strain from military spending.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Osaka Report Concerning Japanese War Trends in the Kwansai

subfiles.about: Reports on popular morale, the capitalist war boom, labor conditions, international disillusionment, and anti-Jewish propaganda in the Kansai region.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Makinson analyzes the domestic impact of the China war in the Kansai industrial district, reporting strong civilian support, lucrative profits for industrialists producing munitions and substitutes, acute labor shortages, and rising wages. He notes, however, growing disillusionment and caution among informed Japanese over American military aid to European democracies and firm talk from Washington. The report also addresses Japanese concerns that foreign press allegations of anti-Semitic discrimination could alienate American finance and damage crucial trade interests like the silk industry.
subfiles.title: Japanese War Trends as Observed in the Kwansai
